title: TrueMapData: one format for measured surfaces

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A scanner measures a coin down to its tiniest bumps. Now how do you use that same measurement in a lab report and in a game engine?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds like two different worlds. Is there one answer for both?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the idea behind TrueMapData. It's a Python library and a command line tool, maintained under ETSim, for height maps from TrueMap and GelSight captures. It reads them as NumPy arrays, so one representation serves both metrology and graphics.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A grid where each cell stores how high the surface is at that spot, plus the spacing between cells. So you keep the physical scale. The library's own file format is just a small header, that spatial information, and the grid of heights.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And once it's loaded, what can you do with it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Look at it first. A 2D heatmap, a 3D surface, profiles along a row or a column, contours, even comparisons between files. Then you can derive things for graphics, like normal maps and displacement maps, or export a mesh, all with the scale preserved.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is it only for pictures, though? You mentioned metrology.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No, it also measures. There's an optional roughness add-on that follows the ISO 25178 standard for areal roughness. And a second command, called tmd-wear, compares captures of the same surface over time.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Wear, like a surface slowly getting scuffed?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. The repository ships three GelSight captures taken after zero, one hundred fifty and three hundred millimetres of sliding at one hundred grams. One command compares them and reports how much material was lost compared with the first capture.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's on PyPI under the name truemapdata, with an MIT licence. You install it with pip, and the page has a short script that builds a two hundred by two hundred height map in memory, saves it, loads it back and crops it, so you don't even need a capture file.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is one surface format that goes from a microscope to a render.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the idea. The full write-up has the example figures and the list of extras.
